title: How Google DeepMind Runs Agents at Scale — KP Sawhney & Ian Ballantyne, Google DeepMind

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 78%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk is primarily about the Antigravity agent harness, deep research agent architecture, multi-agent patterns, and the control plane for managing agents at Google scale. Antigravity is an internal developer platform used by software builders, and the discussion extensively covers enterprise-scale agent operations and quota management across thousands of users. The talk covers building agent harnesses, operating them in production with observability and quota management, and the challenges of evaluating agentic workflows. Requires familiarity with agentic AI concepts and IDE-based development workflows per the stated prerequisites, but remains accessible to practitioners without deep ML expertise. The video is a panel discussion with a live demo and extended audience Q&A as described in the video description and transcript sections. All evidence anchors are graded as said_in_transcript, confirming direct speaker statements throughout the talk.

summary: Ian Ballantyne (developer relations engineer) and KP Sawhney (software engineer in DeepMind's AI platform team) open with a demo of Antigravity, a Visual Studio-style IDE with a full agent manager framework. The agent analyzes files, creates an implementation plan with to-dos, launches a browser, inspects the DOM, captures screenshots or video, and produces a scratch pad. Human-in-the-loop review allows editing the plan before proceeding. KP's deep research agent (available via the interactions API) is being generalized beyond coding; the key architectural shift replaces passing huge text blobs between pipeline components with a shared file system so components collaborate like human researchers and produce supporting artifacts such as infographics and documents. Q&A expands on several areas. Observability uses a custom internal web app with drill-down to raw predict requests and an agent trajectory store that helps diagnose where looping or off-rails behavior begins. Multi-agent systems are not massively parallel today but rather work on different tracks within a project; efficient agent-to-agent communication and human supervisory control are seen as the future. KP strongly prefers skills over MCP, calling MCP possibly a flash in the pan while valuing its auth layer; expert-contributed skills give all employees specialized knowledge for free. Evaluation remains hard—sandboxed environments and fresh datasets are needed, with skill authors and even agents themselves experimenting with test generation. Googlers have worse token limits than paying customers because customers are prioritized; the harness is moving toward seamless fallback across model tiers (pro to flash to local) without interrupting workflows. Automated code review uses per-language auto-review models fine-tuned on style guides plus per-product custom prompts, with tools like Jewels enabling web-based PR review. The ballooning volume of agent-generated code makes automated review increasingly critical.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction of KP Sawhney and Ian Ballantyne
sections.summary: Ian Ballantyne (developer relations engineer) and KP Sawhney (software engineer in DeepMind's AI platform team) introduce themselves and outline the agentic panel format.

sections.title: Demo of the Antigravity agentic platform
sections.summary: Ian demos Antigravity, an IDE with an agent manager framework. The agent implements a spec file by analyzing existing files, creating an implementation plan with to-dos, launching a browser to test the app, inspecting the DOM, capturing screenshots/video, and writing scratch pad notes. Human-in-the-loop review allows editing the plan before proceeding.

sections.title: KP's work with the deep research agent
sections.summary: KP explains his work on the deep research agent (now available via the interactions API) and his current focus on generalizing the Antigravity harness beyond coding. Key architectural shift: replacing huge text blobs passed between pipeline components with a shared file system for human-researcher-like collaboration and artifact production.

sections.title: Skills libraries and managing agent sprawl
sections.summary: KP discusses DeepMind's large internal skills library that helps employees deliver code faster. At Google's scale, skills risk sprawling out of control. They are taking a Darwinian approach where only the best skills survive. Some upcoming capabilities will be revealed at IO.

sections.title: Scalability and token quotas at Google
sections.summary: KP addresses token hunger as the top scaling challenge. Per-user and per-team quota management is critical. Strategies include mixing free Gemma models on own GPUs/TPUs with advanced models for specific components. Evaluation of complex workflows is a focus, including mock TPUs to test harnesses without consuming real compute.

sections.title: Audience Q&A: Managing per-user agent behaviors
sections.summary: KP explains per-user management is currently brute force: power users are told to stop. Google's SRE team monitors clusters 24/7 and directly contacts teams to stop jobs causing spikes. KP notes subscription pricing does not fit token-hungry agentic systems, citing Anthropic blocking open-claw usage as an industry signal.

sections.title: Audience Q&A: Observability and agent trajectory stores
sections.summary: KP describes a custom internal web app for observability that lets users drill down through hierarchy levels to raw predict requests. An agent trajectory store focuses on coding, helping diagnose where looping started or the model went off-rails. KP asks the audience what tools they use for observability.

sections.title: Audience Q&A: Future of deep research pipelines
sections.summary: KP confirms the deep research pipeline is being actively explored for faster, cheaper, better results using the same harness. The current system passes huge context through, which is expensive and consumes context. The vision is making each element a collaborator in a workspace, like human researchers, opening potential for infographics, support artifacts, and documents.

sections.title: Audience Q&A: Handling multi-agent systems
sections.summary: KP explains multi-agent systems are not massively parallel today; agents work on different trains of operation within a project and can overlap on jobs. Efficient agent-to-agent communication and giving humans supervisory control over a digital assembly line is the future direction.

sections.title: Audience Q&A: Perspectives on skills vs. MCP
sections.summary: KP strongly prefers skills, calling MCP possibly a flash in the pan while valuing its auth perspective. Skills plus guardrail CLI interactions work well for him. Expert-contributed skills give all employees specialized knowledge for free. DeepMind supports both and will follow community usage.

sections.title: Audience Q&A: Evaluating agentic workflows
sections.summary: KP says evaluation is hard: spinning up sandboxed environments is mechanically difficult, and coming up with new datasets is the trickiest part. Skill authors bear responsibility for testing, but agents are also being experimented with for designing tests, making it meta.

sections.title: Audience Q&A: Handling model limits and quota management
sections.summary: KP reveals Googlers have worse token limits than paying customers because customers are prioritized. The harness is moving toward seamless fallback across model tiers (pro to flash to local) without interrupting workflows, so hitting a limit does not stall long-running jobs silently.

sections.title: Audience Q&A: Automated code review processes
sections.summary: KP describes per-language auto-review models fine-tuned on style guides and good code examples, plus per-product custom prompts and SRIs. Agents can comment on PRs automatically. Tools like Jewels provide web-based PR review. The ballooning volume of agent-generated code makes automated review increasingly critical.
